result.summary: After their defeat the Messenians suffer from costly garrisons, desertions and a plague, and withdraw to Mount Ithome. An oracle from Delphi demands the sacrifice of a maiden of the Æpytidæ, and after the lot and a substitution fail, Aristodemus kills his own daughter. King Euphaes persuades the people that this fulfilled the oracle.

scenes.title: Messenians retreat to Ithome
scenes.summary: Ruined by costs, desertions and plague, the Messenians abandon their inland towns and fortify Mount Ithome.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians risk ruin and loss of their country to the Lacedæmonians.

scenes.title: Tisis brings the oracle
scenes.summary: Tisis is sent to Delphi and is ambushed by Lacedæmonians on his return. A voice lets him go, and he delivers the oracle to the king before dying of his wounds.
scenes.stakes: Tisis risks death in ambush before delivering the oracle.

scenes.title: The lot and Lyciscus' flight
scenes.summary: The oracle demands a virgin sacrifice. The lot falls on Lyciscus' supposed daughter, but Epebolus exposes her as a substitute and Lyciscus flees to Sparta. Aristodemus offers his own daughter.
scenes.stakes: The Messenians fear the gods' anger and the loss of their country if the oracle is not obeyed.

scenes.title: Aristodemus kills his daughter
scenes.summary: A jealous suitor falsely claims the girl is pregnant, and Aristodemus kills her in a rage. Euphaes persuades the people the oracle is fulfilled.
scenes.stakes: Messene's safety depends on the oracle being satisfied; the suitor risks being killed by the crowd.

notable_quotes.reason: Memorable image of Fate secretly directing human desires like pebbles on a river bottom.

analysis.text: Fate and oracles drive the Messenians to human sacrifice, and Aristodemus' good intention ends in a useless tragedy.
Pausanias draws on the Messenian war tradition, which glorifies Messenian resistance to Sparta, and relates it with Homeric and Delphic authority.

fun_facts.text: Mount Ithome in Messenia is the same Ithome Homer names in the Catalogue of Ships (Iliad 2).

language_notes.text: Homer's catalogue is the list of Greek forces in the Iliad, Book 2, where 'rocky Ithome' appears among the places that sent troops.
'Without any appearance of the speaker' means a disembodied voice, implying divine intervention.
'Gods below' are the underworld deities, who received sacrifices made by night.
'Palmed off' means passed off by trickery; the barren wife had pretended another child was her own.
'Amour' means a love affair; here the suitor falsely claims intimacy with her.
Epebolus argues the killing was not a valid sacrifice, since it was done in anger rather than as a ritual offering to the gods.

context_notes.text: Ithome is a steep mountain in Messenia, a natural fortress; it became the centre of Messenian resistance against Sparta.
Delphi's oracle of Apollo, speaking through the Pythian priestess, was consulted by Greek states before major decisions, especially in war.
The Æpytidæ were a Messenian royal-descended family, which is why the oracle limits the victim to it.

literary_notes.text: Tisis' refusal to be taken alive despite his wounds shows his courage and devotion, marking him as a worthy envoy.
Fate's hidden direction of human desires is compared to pebbles on a riverbed, unseen beneath the surface yet shaping the flow.
Aristodemus kills his daughter in rage over a lie, and the cutting open proves her innocent, making his act cruelly pointless.
Euphaes shields his friend by declaring the oracle fulfilled, so a personal motive shapes the public interpretation of the god's command.
